name: Mossy Green
lede: Mossy Green is a medium, yellowish green that names the color of moss, and the same words turn up in recipes for making a dark green out of old verdigris.

sections.title: Where the name sits
sections.body: In our library Mossy Green is a modern everyday name, listed with the X11/CSS, Wikipedia and xkcd sets and with the ISCC-NBS system of 1955, where it falls in block 110 [1]. Its closest relatives are yellow-greens: the library records Olive Drab and Maximum Green as near-duplicates, each about 2.1 units away, while [[forest-green]] is farther off at 8.5 [1]. The Japanese color Mo'egi (萌黄) is filed beside it [1]. Our sources do not document who first used the English name as a color [1].

sections.title: Mossy green in the studio
sections.body: The books use the words in a more specific way. The Pigment Compendium notes that late medieval manuscripts, among them a fifteenth-century Italian one cited from Merrifield's 1849 work, suggest grinding verdigris with the juice of rue leaves [2]. Modern experiments by Woudhuysen-Keller and Woudhuysen in 1998 found that this turned the blue-green of neutral verdigris into a dark mossy green [2]. The same authors found neutral, recrystallized verdigris more stable in oil than the basic kind [3]. A darker relative is [[sap-green]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 14 of 23,781 paintings [4]. Eight are French, and five come from the 1890s, which has about seven times the archive's rate [4]. The largest share is in Degas's *Racehorses in a Landscape* of 1894, at about 25 per cent, and Pissarro's 1898 [[painting:commons-Q12857030|Place du Theatre-Francais in Spring]] also matches [4]. As photographed: museum photographs of aged, varnished paintings; a color match is not a pigment test.
